utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the Registrar call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-03-68-PT, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: May I have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. For the Prosecution appear Mr. Jayantha Jayasuriya on my right-hand side, trial attorney. Ms. Kimberley Fleming on my left-hand side, trial support. And I, Ekkehard Withopf, acting senior trial attorney.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and assisting Mr. John Jones, defending Mr. Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. And we have the Federation representative here also, I understand. Would you like to introduce yourself, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HALILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my name is Mevludin Halilovic. I'm a Minister of the Interior of the government of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And Bosnia-Herzegovina has been respecting the Tribunal from its founding. It has been closely cooperating with the Tribunal carrying out its requests and saying that it will continue to do so in future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is the hearing of a motion for provisional release by this accused. It has been fully briefed in that we have had full submissions from both sides. We will hear oral submissions, but they shouldn't repeat the matters which are already in the brief. We'll hear from the Defence first, it being their motion.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, following your suggestion, I will not repeat the arguments that we have written down in the submission in our motion for provisional release of Mr. Oric dated 21st of May, 2003, and our response to the Prosecution motion to our response. But because of the heavy accusations that were submitted by the Prosecution, I will have to raise some issues that the Prosecutor has been insisting in his submissions. I will not speak a lot regarding what the Prosecution said, saying that the burden of proof is on the Defence to prove that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down considering that Ms. Vidovic is reading.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything that I am saying in response to the Prosecution motion, the Rule says that release may be granted by the Trial Chamber. I am deeply convinced that the word "may" indicates that the Trial Chamber may grant provisional release under certain conditions which are clearly set out in the Rule. The Chamber must be convinced that the accused, if released, will appear at the trial and that he will not represent a danger to victims, witnesses, or any other persons. The Chamber does not have any other discretionary powers under this Rule. In this case, the Prosecutor has gone so far as to ask that the accused be kept in detention even if the Defence is able to present valid arguments to show that both conditions in Rule 65(B) have been met. They have asked the Trial Chamber to use its right to reject a motion for provisional release. The Prosecutor quotes with approval the claim that detention is needed before a trial in order to maintain the confidence of the public in the fairness of the trial. Your Honours, the Tribunal is applying international law and international legal standards from human rights law which say that detention should be as brief as possible before a trial, and that detention should be -- should be exercised when it is absolutely necessary. This is not in accordance with the interpretation put forward by the Prosecution. Public confidence can only be maintained by a fair trial. All of us here, including the Prosecution, are here to contribute to a fair trial. The Prosecutor must treat the accused fairly. Your Honours, this is not what they're doing. The Prosecution made it impossible for Mr. Oric to surrender voluntarily to the Tribunal. Mr. Oric cooperated with the Prosecution. He was interviewed as an accused on several occasions, and from parts of his interview, which we have adduced, it is evident that he voluntarily gave the interviews which lasted, in our estimation, about 105 hours. On the 6th of April, 2001, he told the investigators that if indicted, he wanted to surrender to The Hague voluntarily. The police commissioner of Tuzla Mr. Divkovic, as can be seen from our annex C, made the statement which shows that the accused did apply to the police asking for it to be made possible to surrender voluntarily. However, SFOR was ordered to arrest him by force quite unnecessarily, and it is this lack of necessity that caused such public indignation and outrage. The same public that the Prosecution has in mind. Your Honours, Mr. Oric's surrender was accepted. It was to be voluntary, so this sounds cynical. They say his surrender was voluntary, but this has nothing to do with whether he would be willing to attend the trial, to be at the trial after seeing the evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You needn't argue that point further because they have conceded that he is to be treated as if he did, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, they have conceded voluntarily, but now they are saying that he will not appear at his trial because certain circumstances could influence the government and it will not be able to arrest him. Your Honours, articles have been presented about public protests in Tuzla which were broadcast on CNN and other TV stations and published in the press. Please look at all this carefully. The contents of these reports are one thing, and the Prosecutor's interpretation is quite another. They are trying to give these reports a meaning they do not have. Both texts adduced by the Prosecution say that several hundred mothers and wives of the victims of the terrible massacre in Srebrenica in 1995 protested, and it's evident from both articles that they protested not because Oric was arrested but because Karadzic and Mladic have not been arrested. And these are key figures accused of the genocide. One of the articles says that the key figures accused of the massacres are still at large. The women of Srebrenica, after a funeral in the village of Potocari, where hundreds of victims of this massacre were buried, said in this article: "We demanded that Karadzic and Mladic be arrested as soon as possible. Instead of this, one of our people has been arrested." It is evident further from the article that the mothers of Srebrenica protest on the 11th day of every month. The essence of these protests is something far more serious. Please bear in mind something that the Prosecution has neglected to mention. The protests, when they took place in front of the UN, it was Mr. Oric who himself came out to calm down the protesters. And we have adduced a document showing this, which shows what his attitude is both to the protests and to international justice. On this occasion, I want to draw attention to some major contradictions between the evidence put forward by the Prosecution and the conclusion the Prosecution draws from this evidence. First of all, they say that Oric is considered a hero in his environment and that the government will have serious difficulties if they wish to fulfill their guarantees because of the protest campaign that has been mentioned. However, in developing their arguments on the danger that the accused would pose to witnesses, victims, and other persons, they say, referring to Oric, the following: "People who were killed or who took part in the clashes were members of his family or his subordinates." Then they adduce a statement by an anonymous witness describing the protests against Oric in Srebrenica. The pamphlets issued against him. The evidence provided by the Prosecution compromise their own conclusions. Furthermore, the conclusions drawn by the Prosecution about the importance of the accused and his status as a hero in Srebrenica are incorrect, or it is the witness statements that they themselves provide that are incorrect. It is up to Your Honours to make the decision, the right decision on this. As regards to the protest by the mothers of Srebrenica, I have adduced a letter which is a guarantee that they will refrain from anything that might compromise the decision made by the government to fulfill all their obligations to this Tribunal. I will remind you briefly once again that we have put forward a number of newspaper articles from which it is evident that on the occasion of the arrest of all Bosniak generals, there were always protests, including protests by the mothers of Srebrenica, and Oric is no exception to this. Especially large protests were held in Sanski Most when 15.000 citizens of this town protested when General Alagic was arrested. Numerous citizens' associations in Bosnia and Herzegovina protested but this did not hinder the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina from providing guarantees that they will again arrest the general, and it did not hinder them from performing all their undertakings. The government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I assert, will fulfill all their guarantees, and the Tribunal should have no reserves in accepting these guarantees. The cooperation of official Sarajevo and the Tribunal has been ongoing ever since the Tribunal was founded. It has always been unconditional. In November 1994, an agreement was signed with the Prosecution on the handing over of evidence and accused to The Hague Tribunal. The war was still going on when this happened. The government of Bosnia and Herzegovina recognised the right of the Tribunal to issue subpoenas and they undertook to comply with these in the Blaskic case. Arrests on the orders of the Court took place immediately when Landzo and Delic were arrested. They were handed over to the jurisdiction of the Tribunal, as were the leading figures in the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Hadzialijagic and Hadzihasanovic. There is no arrest warrant that the government of the Federation did not execute immediately. And finally, the government of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina in its -- in Article 8 of its constitution under the Dayton Accords is bound to cooperate with the Tribunal and carry out all its orders. There is no guarantee provided by the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina that will not be carried out and no person that will not be handed over because of public pressure. All this runs counter to the claims by the Prosecution. The Prosecution claim that the accused, if released, would pose a danger to victims, witnesses, or any other persons is without any foundation whatsoever. The Prosecution bases their claim on the alleged previous behaviour of the accused. They say that it is well known that many individuals who spoke out against the activities of the accused suffered serious consequences, including death under mysterious circumstances. First of all, what does it mean when they say this is well known? What does this mean and what does death in mysterious circumstances mean? This speaks for itself. The Prosecution goes on to say that the accused and his accomplices instigated a reign of terror and that no one was allowed to doubt their activities. Does this not run counter to the argument of the Prosecution that the accused is considered a hero in his environment? In paragraphs 12, 13, 14, and 15 of their response, they base all this on disinformation, rumour, gossip, and insinuation. The Prosecutor has completely forgotten the presumption of innocence which is guaranteed in Article 21(3) of the Statute. The accused is not to be considered guilty until proved guilty. The main proof of the violent behaviour of the accused is found by the Prosecution in a state security document entitled "Naser Oric, information and indications." For lawyers, the very title "information and indications" means a lot. However, in footnote number 12, the Prosecution say that this document is the result of an investigation, and this was submitted to the commander of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is simply not true. On page 8 of this document, under "conclusions and proposals," items 3 and 4, it is evident that this document is only a basis for an investigation, that this is a pre-investigation document, and that the investigation authorities are only to begin collecting information and evidence and throwing light on these indications. However, let us take a look at this document. It is replete with indications and insinuation. On page 3, under number 4, it says: "Oric detained some witnesses who were killed under mysterious circumstances." In 5, it says that, "The former SDA president and the head of the Srebrenica SMB was injured under mysterious circumstances." Then the civilian protection commissioner also allegedly knew of Oric's machinations. Under number 8, it says that Aljukic, before the war, had a company, but this was not verified. Then it says that allegedly, there were murders which were never cleared up. In 19, it says: "According to unverified information, Oric has an account in Paris." So everything is alleged, everything is unverified, everything is not clear. Yesterday, Your Honours, the Prosecution delivered to us in the late afternoon two additional documents, one of which is a document of the Tuzla State Security Service dated the 12th of January, 1996. First of all, I wish to draw attention to the fact that the English text, which is a translation from Bosnian into English, should be taken with a large grain of salt. A superficial comparison of the original text and the translation shows that during the translation into English, mistakes were made which changed the meaning of the document considerably. On pages 3 and 4, items 9, 10, 11, 14, 15, and 18, when a name is mentioned, for example, Begic, in the original, it says "A certain Begic, a man called Begic" which in the original points to the lack of information about this person. In the English text, it just says "Begic," making it appear that the -- who this person is is quite clear. In the translation into English, which was handed over by the Prosecution, it says on page 8, it is page 5 of the Bosnian original, "After the arrival in Tuzla, Oric received 500.000 deutschmarks," while in the original, it says: "Oric allegedly received 500.000 deutschmarks." Your Honours, that is a significant difference. Received, if we say received, that has been established. But when we say allegedly received, that means that somebody may have said that Oric may have received this amount of money. Your Honours, I do want to believe that these mistakes happened because the translation of the document was rushed. The entire document is replete with such mistakes, and I will have to stress another important one on page 9 where it says that, according to the English text, it says: "According to a certain Rifat Suljic from Polje Visnjica" while in the original, it says: "According to the reactions of a certain man called Rifat," when we use the word "certain," that means that he came and gave a statement. He told something to someone. But if we say that it's somebody's reaction, then it has a completely different, more general meaning. So I would like the Prosecutor to hand over to the Trial Chamber an adequate translation. I want to say something about this document. The document as it is, as we were given it by the Prosecutor, is about the same as the document dated the 23rd of September, 1995. It is also called "information or intelligence" and it's also speaking about unchecked, uncorroborated information about certain murders, about intelligence given by some unknown persons, and some events that are mentioned, for instance, the wounding of Mr. Mustafic. It says that on the same page, that it is possible that Mr. Mustafic could have been wounded by one of Naser's men, Naser Oric. And it also says that rumour has it that for the same event may have been caused by a man called Mrki Mandzo. Now what kind of documents are these? As far as Oric himself is concerned, this document such as it is, there is no way that this document says at any point that Naser Oric is dangerous. Specifically, in relation to Mr. Oric, on page 1, this document specifically under items 8, 9, and 10 it, says allegedly he may have received a certain amount of money. That certain people close to him may have sold flour to him from humanitarian aid. There are other things in there, other rumours, but there is nothing about things that are relevant to this case. Now, in this document, there is a general assessment on page 8 that the leaders of the 28th Division were anarchic and that in every way they discredited and prevented the work of civilian authority, civilian organs by force. Now this comment, Your Honours, when we look at the context in reference to Mr. Oric, cannot be brought into connection with Mr. Oric. Now, very briefly, I will speak about the second document that was added by the Prosecutor dated 10th of March, 1997, from the same source. And this document speaks about the ending on the investigation, or rather, that the planned tasks have been carried out, and what is proposed is the closing of the file. In fact, it says that at -- what should happen, the plan action should be terminated. Your Honours, naturally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can I ask, did you give a comprehensive list just now of the mistakes in translation?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe I have. Perhaps not a complete list. I said that it was a cursory analysis of the translation. I didn't really have time for that, Your Honours, because I received the document late afternoon yesterday. I just pointed to those mistakes that changed the meaning, that altered the meaning, particularly considering that the translation has been done to the detriment of my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when speaking about the documents submitted by the Prosecution, Prosecutor's document, I would like to say further that on the basis of such documents, the Prosecutor wishes to represent Mr. Oric as being a dangerous murderer who is terrorising and causing fear, and that therefore he will be dangerous for victims and witnesses. Your Honours, in these documents, these documents do not give any basis to the Prosecutor to state such things. There is a lot in information and indication in this document, this is not a result of an investigation which has been carried out, as it has been suggested by the Prosecutor. In order to check this, I have carried out very detailed investigations, and I have also added the statement of General Jusuf Jasarevic, which is in annex 6 of our submission, which sheds quite a lot of light on things. General Jasarevic is very decisive in saying that it is in connection to this document there has been an overall investigation that was carried out, and according to the data that I have, this investigation of Mr. Oric lasted from 1995 until September 1998 when it was filed in the archive. And this was an overall investigation, all-encompassing. And it did not confirm what has been alleged in the document, and that is why criminal proceedings were never instigated. The criminal proceedings was instigated against Mr. Oric or any other people who were mentioned in the document. From the statement given by Mr. Jasarevic we can, however, see that the investigation has demonstrated there has been a rivalry and conflicts between certain individuals. And as a result of that, this very contradictory information reached the army intelligence service. Now, Your Honours, so that we can establish the truth and to shed light on these facts for the Trial Chamber, we have submitted evidence regarding the interfactional conflicts in Srebrenica at the time. These interfaction clashes, particularly supported by our annex number 7, which is a letter of Mr. Rasim Delic to the Srebrenica citizens, and in this letter, Mr. Delic speaks of his concern because of the clashes among the leaders in Srebrenica. In our annex number 8, in the statement of Mr. Ramiz Becirovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Vidovic, we don't have unlimited time. We can read the various materials that you have. I must ask you, in order that everybody else can have time, to draw to a close, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. Very well. Your Honours, I am doing this because of the seriousness of the accusations, because sometimes they go over what has been set out in the indictment. Very briefly, I will further say that the Prosecutor believes, has been trying to prove, that Mr. Oric has already contacted and trying to influence certain witnesses. Mr. Oric refused any contact with any potential witnesses. He's also refuted the evidence of the statement given by COO2. We gave the affidavit, the statement of Tursunovic where it is stated quite clearly that he's denying what Witness C002 has stated, and I'm not going to go back and stress and quote this. But I would like to ask the Prosecutor whether he believes his Witness C002 because it is a fact that it is the Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not a matter for the Prosecutor to state such things. It's a matter for the Trial Chamber. Now, we're not in a position to try these matters. We're going to have to deal with them on the papers. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Your Honours. I can just add further that other allegations of the Prosecutor are unfounded, that Mr. Oric tried to shift the responsibility and the blame on the dead. This doesn't stand at all. This Prosecutor is basing this on the few pages of his statement. Mr. Oric gave about 2.000 pages worth of statement. And just to extract such a short part of the statement out of context isn't fair. Now, it is certain that a lot of people are among the dead in Srebrenica, and that is the truth, and the Prosecutor should open his eyes to this. Now, on the basis of the proof that the Prosecutor presented on the part of the deliberate campaign of misinformation, particularly when there is so much evidence presented by us which is contrary, now to do so is to deny the presumption of innocence. Now, I will just raise something else very briefly, and this is regarding a person has -- this is in relation to a person for whom the government of BH --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution objects to Mrs. Vidovic to Defence counsel continuing in the manner she does. She has several times been advised by Your Honours that there is nothing about repetition, there is nothing about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, Mr. Withopf, please, it's a matter for the Trial Chamber to determine how long she goes on. But would you have in mind the clock, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honours. I will finish very briefly. Mr. Oric is a person for whom the government gave a very full guarantee, also guaranteed by the police commissioner from Tuzla, that he will appear at his trial. Certainly, as the first man of the local police would not guarantee such a thing for a person who has no respect of law, as he has been presented by the Prosecution. If you look at our annex, and the statement of Mr. Desnica, I can just tell you briefly who this is. Mr. Desnica is the vice-president of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He's a Serb, and he is the first prime minister of the post-war Srebrenica government. And looking at the request for guarantee of Federation of BH, he said: "I know Mr. Oric, and I know what kind of man he is. And because of Srebrenica, it would be good to respect this guarantee." It would be very unlikely that Mr. Desnica could give such a statement in reference to such a person if he didn't have -- if he wasn't sure that Mr. Oric would be respecting the law. Now, I would like to point out another fact which I believe that shows and demonstrates the unfair position towards Mr. Oric of the Prosecution. Now, 42 witnesses live in Republika Srpska. There were 40 statements. Now, in reality, if the accused went into contact with them, there is only one witness who lives in Sarajevo, and this is in -- and he's a witness to general circumstances which has nothing much to do with Mr. Oric. Five are protected witnesses, so -- and there were -- such statements are so -- many large parts of the statements are expunged, so what kind of danger would Mr. Oric present to such witnesses if he doesn't have any data as to who they are? I'm absolutely certain that the Prosecutor is aware of these facts that I have raised, but I believe that the Prosecutor has another objective which has nothing to do with justice and fair trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You will not attribute false motives to the Prosecution. Now, Mr. Halilovic, have you anything you want to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. HALILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is a great honour for me to speak on behalf of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it is on the basis of pursuant to the law of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina the government is guaranteeing that Mr. Naser Oric, if he is provisionally release, he will respect the following conditions upon arrival in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Within three days, he will send the address to the Registrar of the Tribunal. And in case this address is changed, he will inform the Registrar. To the relevant ministry, he will hand over his passport, which will be either kept at the ministry or at the Prosecutor's office in Sarajevo. He will not leave the territory of the Tuzla canton. Once a week, he will report to the Tuzla police. He will consent to having officials of the Federation verify his presence at occasions unannounced visits to the accused by these officials or by a person designated by the Registrar of the Tribunal. He also guarantees that he will not have any contacts whatsoever or in any way interfere with victims or potential witnesses or in otherwise interfere in any way with the proceedings or with the administration of justice. He will not seek access to documents and archives. He will not discuss his case with anyone, including the media, other than his counsel and immediate members of his family. He will not occupy any official position in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Within three days of the start of employment, he will report to the Registrar and include of the position occupied as well as the name and address of the employer. He will strictly comply with any requirements of the authorities of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina necessary to enable them to comply with their obligations under the order for provisional release and the guarantees. He will return to the Tribunal at such time and such date as the Trial Chamber may order. He will strictly comply with any order of the Trial Chamber varying the terms of or terminating the provisional release of the accused. The government of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina are fully going to cooperate with the Tribunal in The Hague and will take over any transport expenses of the accused from Schiphol airport to the place of residence and back. Also, the cost of the personal security and safety of the accused whilst on provisional release. Report immediately to the Registrar of the Tribunal substance of any threats to the security of the accused including full reports of the investigations related to such threats. Facilitate at the request of the Trial Chamber of all the parties all means of cooperation and communication between the parties and ensuring -- and will ensure the confidentiality of any such communication. They will submit a written report to the Registrar of the Tribunal every month as to the presence of the accused and his compliance with the terms of this order. Will immediately detain the accused should he breach any of the terms and conditions of his provisional release and will report immediately any such breach to the Trial Chamber. I have here the authorisation of my government which enabled me to read these through, and I am ready to answer any questions you may have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution will try to answer the different issues that have been addressed by the Defence in a structured manner, focussing on the real factual issues. I will first very, very briefly address the ICTY's jurisprudence, then we will discuss the two relevant reports, the 1995 report and the 1996 report, and finally we will address the government guarantee. The law and the jurisprudence of the Tribunal in respect to Rule 65(B) is summarised as follows: "A decision regarding provisional release pursuant to this Rule involves findings of fact as to whether the accused will appear for trial and whether, if released, he will not pose a danger to any victim, witness, or any other person." It is settled Appeals Chamber jurisprudence that only after finding that the applicant met his burden on those points, the Trial Chamber would exercise its discretion as to whether the applicant should be granted provisional release. The standard is balance of probabilities, there's even ICTY jurisprudence that states that the standard should be a higher one. When it comes to the second prong of Rule 65(B), the jurisprudence of this Tribunal recognises an almost absolute burden of the accused to show an absence of danger to others. Finally, upon exercise of the Trial Chamber's discretion, an applicant may be denied provisional release even if he has met his burden of proof on the two points as set out above. These are the preconditions for any decision on the provisional release application of the accused. The Prosecution will now address the two crucial reports that in the view of the Prosecution show that they are -- its indication that interfere with witnesses, the first report is the 20 September, 1995, report of the military security service of the 2nd Corps signed by Mr. Jusuf Jasarevic, and the second report is the 12th January, 1996, report of the State Security Service in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's make sure that we have these. The first report --

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The first report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a minute. Let me just find it. Which attachment is it to your response?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The first report, Your Honour, is the attachment B to the Prosecution's response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And this is a report of the 2nd Corps? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: That's a report of the military -- this is the report of the military security service of the 2nd Corps of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: ABiH 2nd Corps, right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And the second report is the 12th January 1996 report which has been filed as an annex to our yesterday's filing. This report is a report of the State Security Service in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The Prosecution wishes to emphasise that both Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 27 to 30. reports are official reports of authorities within Bosnia and Herzegovina; they are not gossip, as discredited by the Defence. In respect to these two reports, the Prosecution submits that in particular, the 23rd September report, September 1995 report, can be used in assessing the situation in the context of the provisional release application. Despite the statement of Mr. Jasarevic as provided by the Defence and despite the fact that the accused hasn't been charged for the following reasons: There are legal reasons and there are factual reasons. In regard to the assessment to be made in the context of deciding on provisional release, there is no legal requirement that the information on misconduct of the applicant must have resulted in a judgement against the accused. The Prosecution, therefore, submits that the presumption of innocence is not applicable in this context. The respective Defence arguments are obviously missing the point because the matter to decide is not whether the accused was convicted for the crimes as detailed in the reports; the real matter is whether the information available indicates as to whether the accused may pose a threat to victims, witnesses, or other persons. Coming to the factual reasons, there are at least, at the very least, eight factual reasons to take the 1995 report into consideration. And such reasons are the following ones: Number 1, Mr. Jasarevic's statement is a statement of a private person in his personal capacity. It is not an official statement of a state authority. The Prosecution stresses that the fact that the Defence did not provide a statement by the relevant authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina, what would have been the normal cause of action, and the Prosecution raises the question why not? Second issue, the Prosecution notes that the statement of Mr. Jasarevic very contrary to the Defence submission is vague, it is extremely vague, and not helpful in any respect. Just to illustrate this, I refer to the following quote: "During the processing, it has been found that in Srebrenica in some periods of the war, there are certain conflicts and intolerance amongst certain individuals, and the initial information and findings were contradictory." Such a statement means nothing. What are "certain conflicts" and which certain individuals are concerned? Number 3, the 1995 report, that shows that the authors, including Mr. Jasarevic took it serious. The 1995 report went to the highest authorities, namely to the commander of the general staff of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina to decide and also suggested the arrest of the accused. I refer to page 10, number 6. The report itself asserts and contradicts the assertions made by the Defence, the report itself distinguishes between verified and unverified information. I in particular refer to page 8, paragraph 19. That leads to the conclusion that all allegations that are not specifically identified as unverified information are to be considered as verified information. The Prosecution, as number 5, also notes that Mr. Jasarevic's statement tries to address the reason why the accused hasn't been charged. It, however, does not address the issues relevant to the provisional release application, namely, that the accused by all means and obviously successfully interfered with witnesses. The Prosecution also notes that Mr. Jasarevic states that the information and findings were contradictory. He does not say that the allegations have been proven to not be true. That means even if the Trial Chamber would accept Mr. Jasarevic's statement, there would still be sufficient reason to not be satisfied that the accused will not pose a danger to victims, witnesses, or any other person. Furthermore, the Prosecution wishes to emphasise that also the statement of Mr. Jasarevic suggests that at the end of their proceedings, there was conflicting and therefore not sufficient evidence to charge the accused, there is OTP evidence, namely sensitive source Witness C001, which in crucial portions, I refer to the killing of Nermin Rizvanovic, and the accused's involvement, corroborates the allegations made against the accused. Even the materials submitted by the Defence, the statement of Mr. Ramiz Becirovic, and the report of Rasim Delic, confirm portions of the allegations made in that 1995 report. And finally, the report of the State Security Service, the 1996 report, which has been submitted yesterday, contrary to the statement of Mr. Jasarevic, confirms that investigations, this time initiated by a different body which obviously got the very same information against the accused were conducted throughout 1996. In that context, the Prosecution refers to paragraphs 12, 17, and 19 of the report, also and in particular, to the statement made on page 8 of the 1996 report which reads as follows: "One should take into consideration that the anarchy of the 28th Division leaders who caused fear in leading individuals of the administration of justice and members of the AGB Srebrenica creates aggravating circumstances for the police force in resolving some of the cases." These factual points result in the following situation: There are two very comprehensive, very detailed, and official reports by two different state authorities on the one hand side; and there's a very vague, very vague, hardly connected, and mainly beside the point statement of a private person lacking the overview and information the relevant state authorities would have. What are the relevant allegations about and relevant are the allegations which show that the accused would interfere with victims, witnesses, and other persons. On page 3, paragraph 3, it's mentioned that those individuals have committed several activities following Oric's order. The 1995 report continues on page 3, paragraph 4, again under the heading "information," he also forbid members of the 28th Division to give any kind of statement to the 2nd Corps military security service and the MUP. Therefore, out of fear, majority of combatants unwillingly spoke or didn't speak at all about the observations concerning Oric and his associates. Paragraph 5 -- paragraph 4, sorry, on page 5, under the heading indications, it's mentioned and detailed that Mr. Oric put two key witnesses behind bars. The report continues describing very similar situations on page 5, under paragraph 5. And it mentions that after they were prevented by Oric's men from investigating the case, it is worth emphasising that Oric has provided an apartment in Tuzla for the aforementioned young guards in paying 100 deutschmarks for rent. And finally on page 9, paragraph 1, it's again emphasised, and that's again a quote: "However, most of them are afraid of possible revenge of the group around Oric in case they need to testify in potential trial proceedings." This information obviously in main portions speaking for itself shows the following: The accused is a person, the accused is a person who successfully used each and every available means from using force to using bribery, to interfere with witnesses. The accused is also a person who is in a position to instigate others to use such means. There is no reason to believe why now and in the context of the proceedings before this Tribunal, the accused would not do exactly the same, namely, to pose a substantial danger to victims, witnesses, and any other person. This is the submission of the Prosecution in respect to the two documents. The Prosecution would like to submit a further document today. And in this context, the Prosecution wishes to request closed session, since this is a document that has been provided under the condition that it will only be discussed in closed session, and the Prosecution considers it be necessary under the interests of justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you given a copy to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Yes, the Prosecution provided a copy to the Defence. It's worth to mention that the Prosecution got this document five minutes prior to today's proceedings, and immediately handed over copies to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do apologise, but as I, too, have a document, I would like to introduce in private session for reasons of justice. Because should I present it in open session, it would be detrimental to my further investigations, and it is directly connected to the document just mentioned by the Prosecution. And for this reason, I ask that we remain in closed session for a few minutes longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Has the Defence got a copy of this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll hear you at the end and we will go into private session during that and you can produce the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The Prosecution wishes to finish its statements with submissions in respect to the guarantee of the government of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Since it has been raised by the Defence, the Prosecution wants to make it very clear from the outset, the Prosecution appreciates the good cooperation of the government of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina with the Office of the Prosecutor. The issue in question, however, here is not whether the government is willing to comply with its undertakings; the Prosecution has no doubt that the government wants to comply with its undertakings. But the issue, the real issue, is whether the government is able to do so, and in that respect, there's a serious, a very serious, doubt. Such a doubt that the result has the result that only little and certainly not sufficient weight can be attributed to the present guarantee. There are two issues involved which we would like to address now, and in this context, the Prosecution will have to ask a number of questions to the representative of the government of the Federation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're not going to ask him any questions now. But you can make submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: It's settled Trial Chambers and Appeals Chamber jurisprudence that a government guarantee must be determined in relation to the particular circumstances which arise in a particular case. The Trial Chamber may accept such a guarantee in relation to the accused A, it may, however, not accept such a guarantee in relation to a different accused. That means the weight to be attributed to guarantees by a government depends on a great deal on the circumstances of the applicant. The jurisprudence makes it meaningless, makes meaningless the attempt of the Defence to argue that all accused of Bosniak origin have to be treated in the very same way, which applies to the accused Halilovic, Hadzihasanovic and Kubura. What applies to them does not necessarily have to apply to the accused Naser Oric. The Prosecution raises the issue as to whether the representative of the government of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina was aware of the reports that have been discussed at length during the hearing, the 1995 report, the 1996 report, and it raises the question whether the representatives of the government or the government itself would have provided the very same guarantee if they would have been aware of these two reports. And the Prosecution also raises the question whether the guarantee, taking into account the fact that the accused is, and that's not disputed by the Defence, is considered being a war hero and has many, many contacts to many third persons and has the ability to use whatever means as to whether the government of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, under such circumstances, is actually able to control the accused and to control the provisional release conditions as it has been set out by the representative of the government of the Federation. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Vidovic or Mr. Jones, whoever wants to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. May it please Your Honour, I'll be replying to the Prosecution's response briefly. I would like to deal with the two reports referred to by the Prosecution which, in fact, aren't really by the nature of being reports but rather preliminary indications as is clear from their face. But I'll come to that in a moment, I just wanted to preface my remarks with a couple of general remarks in response to the Prosecution. The very first remark I'd like to make is that it should have become clear to Your Honours there has been extremely late service of documents by the Prosecution and the report which the Prosecution is now heavily relying on, 1996 the report, was, in fact, only filed yesterday as Your Honours have seen, and our application, as Your Honour is aware, was made on the 21st of May. The Prosecution responded on the 3rd of June. We replied again on the 13th of June. There's now been a hearing scheduled for two weeks and it's only just now that the Prosecution is coming forward at the eleventh hour with these documents. And that's something which Your Honour, I would submit, you should take into account. As regards the jurisprudence of this Tribunal being settled as a matter of on whom the burden lies, I respectfully submit that in fact the position is not nearly as clear as the Prosecution would like. In fact, the jurisprudence is quite varied. There is dissenting opinion indeed by Your Honour, Judge Robinson, in the Krajisnik case on the 8th of October, 2001, and paragraph 30 of which Your Honour says that there will be no perils to the Tribunal's mandate if the burden under Rule 65 were on the Prosecution not to the Defence. There's a very strongly worded dissenting opinion of Judge hunt which was referred to in footnote 3 of our reply. And there is the Hadzihasanovic, Alagic and Kubura decisions on provisional release of 19th of December, 2001, in which the Trial Chamber held that any system of per se detention was contrary to international human rights norms, and that decision hasn't been overturned by the Appeals Chamber. So I would submit that it's not a settled question of law on whom the burden lies. I would leave it to the Trial Chamber in rendering a decision in this matter to set the appropriate test. Just as a general point again before addressing the Prosecution's remarks, I would refer Your Honours to the Tadic judgement of the 7th of May, 1997 where in a different context, admittedly, the Trial Chamber stated that where, in fact, there are two conclusions which are open to be drawn by the Chamber given sentences --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Jones slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My apologies. I'll slow down. Where there are two conclusions which can be drawn and which are fairly even balanced, it is not open to the Trial Chamber to draw the conclusion least favourable to the accused. Perhaps it's less a question of a presumption of innocence, but really that that the accused should always have the benefit of the doubt. And essentially, in this case what we're presented with is two possibilities: Either Mr. Oric is the monster that he has been made out to be by the Prosecution or there is, as the documents attest, or there has been a campaign of disinformation and misinformation and that that's the cause of these allegations which are, in fact, baseless, and we submit it's the latter, and clearly the latter, and the documents support that. The point is also not whether or not the accused, Mr. Oric, has been convicted of any crimes. It's not certainly a requirement that he has been convicted of a crime before the Chamber can have any regard to any charges. The point is that Mr. Oric is of good character, he has no criminal convictions, neither do any of his alleged associates have any convictions, and therefore his credibility shouldn't be prejudged. The Chamber, I would submit, should approach it with an open mind and consider that Mr. Oric may very well be telling the truth in his affidavit and that these allegations are, as I say, without foundation. Finally, I apologise for these preliminary comments, but I think it's necessary just to set the context, we are also not submitting that all Bosniaks should be treated the same. That's not the point. The point is that in Hadzihasanovic, Mehmed Alagic, and Amir Kubura, Sefer Halilovic, were all granted bail, largely based on the fact that their bail was underwritten or guaranteed by a reliable and cooperative government, namely the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And we would submit that Mr. Oric should be treated in that same -- in the same category. And the only thing which is coming between Mr. Oric and provisional release are these allegations which the Prosecution have raised. And so that's what we obviously have to turn our minds to. And so there are these two reports which the Prosecution refers to, the 1995 report and the 1996 report. Your Honours, the 1995 report, as I said, is not actually a report at all. It's clearly indicated on its face that it's, as my learned friend Ms. Vidovic said, it's a pre-investigation, if you like. And the point about our response to that, General Jasarevic's rebuttal, if you like, in which he said that those indications were found to be baseless after an extensive investigation involving phone tapping and other investigative techniques, his conclusion was that there was nothing to pursue. There was nothing there. And the point is not that General Jasarevic is a private citizen and we should have sought some official rebuttal; the point is that General Jasarevic was the very person who signed off on the 1995 report, so he's the very person to go back to explain what the follow-up was. And his explanation is there was no follow-up because there was no basis for going any further for bringing criminal proceedings. The file, in other words, was closed. And on the 1996 report, let me just turn to that, there also there's a document, and may I just check with my learned friend whether we need to go into closed session with respect to that document or not. We have a document which also indicates that no criminal proceedings were investigated after that investigation by that body, because as the Prosecution has pointed out, this appears to have been an investigation by a different body, namely, the State Security Service. And in fact, we have a document from the same security service in which they, too, concluded that there was nothing to -- no proceedings to institute, nothing to follow up upon. And then finally, Your Honours, we have a document, and this is a document which we will need to go into private session, which speaks to this issue of misinformation and disinformation. So if we might just pass now into private session briefly and I can address you as to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecution has sought in discussing the guarantees offered by the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina to drive a wedge between what the government is willing to do and what the government is able to do. Well, with respect, Your Honour, a government doesn't come forward and make frivolous guarantees which it doesn't consider itself to be in a position to fulfill. The government of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina is only giving those guarantees with the knowledge that it's able to carry them out. And it's ironic that, in fact, these fears of intimidation of witnesses which the Prosecution is drawing attention to all allegedly stem from investigations carried out by Bosnian organs; and yet, the Bosnian state, the Federation, in any event, is coming here today and saying that they essentially don't have, don't share those fears, that in fact it would be perfectly workable and perfectly acceptable for Mr. Oric to be bailed. And the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina is, one might say, the oldest friend of this Tribunal, in that it has cooperated from the beginning, has always carried out arrests of its own citizens from the beginning, has always cooperated with the service of documents -- with providing documents to this Court. And so, Your Honour, I would submit that the most fundamental consideration possibly is the fact that the government is willing to offer these guarantees which in fact belies all of the submissions the Prosecution has made about these various risks and concerns which are out there. And finally, Your Honour, actually just on the letter which was produced today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honours. Finally just with respect to this letter produced today from (redacted), firstly, there's no allegation there that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sorry, can we please ask for closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. In summary, then my submission is that Mr. Oric is a safe bet, if you like, for provisional release. You can be satisfied that if released he wouldn't pose a danger to any witnesses, he wouldn't pose a danger in terms of intimidation of witnesses, and would certainly not seek to flee. And unless I can assist you further, those would be my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't know if Mr. Halilovic you want to add anything since some comments were made by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HALILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the government of the Federation based its written guarantee on the previous guarantee and assessment of the local police headed by Commissioner Divkovic so that with a reference to whether the government can provide these guarantees, the government has undertaken to do so in writing and is prepared to provide any further guarantees that the Trial Chamber may require.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Was the government aware of the two reports at the time when it made -- gave the guarantee?

utterances.speaker: MR. HALILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The government was not aware of these two reports, but this does not mean that the local police did not have these reports available to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. The Trial Chamber will consider this matter and give its decision in due course in writing. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just get one minute --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've heard everybody, Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I only would like to respond to the annex which has been handed over immediately prior to today's oral hearing. Are we still in private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, we're not. We should go into private session to do it.
